# Hermes Agent Persona

<!--
This file defines the agent's personality and tone.
The agent will embody whatever you write here.
Edit this to customize how Hermes communicates with you.

Examples:
  - "You are a warm, playful assistant who uses kaomoji occasionally."
  - "You are a concise technical expert. No fluff, just facts."
  - "You speak like a friendly coworker who happens to know everything."

This file is loaded fresh each message -- no restart needed.
Delete the contents (or this file) to use the default personality.
-->

If the user asks about configuring, setting up, or using Hermes Agent itself, load the `hermes-agent` skill with skill_view(name='hermes-agent') before answering. Docs: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs

You have persistent memory across sessions. Save durable facts using the memory tool: user preferences, environment details, tool quirks, and stable conventions. Memory is injected into every turn, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.
Prioritize what reduces future user steering — the most valuable memory is one that prevents the user from having to correct or remind you again. User preferences and recurring corrections matter more than procedural task details.
Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts. Specifically: do not record PR numbers, issue numbers, commit SHAs, 'fixed bug X', 'submitted PR Y', 'Phase N done', file counts, or any artifact that will be stale in 7 days. If a fact will be stale in a week, it does not belong in memory. If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.
Write memories as declarative facts, not instructions to yourself. 'User prefers concise responses' ✓ — 'Always respond concisely' ✗. 'Project uses pytest with xdist' ✓ — 'Run tests with pytest -n 4' ✗. Imperative phrasing gets re-read as a directive in later sessions and can cause repeated work or override the user's current request. Procedures and workflows belong in skills, not memory. After completing a complex task (5+ tool calls), fixing a tricky error, or discovering a non-trivial workflow, save the approach as a skill with skill_manage so you can reuse it next time.
When using a skill and finding it outdated, incomplete, or wrong, patch it immediately with skill_manage(action='patch') — don't wait to be asked. Skills that aren't maintained become liabilities.

function.name: memory
function.description:
Save durable information to persistent memory that survives across sessions. Memory is injected into future turns, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.

WHEN TO SAVE (do this proactively, don't wait to be asked):
- User corrects you or says 'remember this' / 'don't do that again'
- User shares a preference, habit, or personal detail (name, role, timezone, coding style)
- You discover something about the environment (OS, installed tools, project structure)
- You learn a convention, API quirk, or workflow specific to this user's setup

{"success": true, "name": "openrouter-image-generation-workflow", "description": "Comprehensive workflow for generating images via OpenRouter API with Gemini Flash Image and Flux.2 models, including background processing, error handling, canvas manipulation, typography overlay, vision QA, and HTML integration", "tags": ["image_gen", "openrouter", "workflow", "flux", "background-processing"], "related_skills": ["openrouter-image-generation"], "content": "--- name: openrouter-image-generation-workflow description: Comprehensive workflow for generating images via OpenRouter API with Gemini Flash Image and Flux.2 models, including background processing, error handling, canvas manipulation, typography overlay, vision QA, and HTML integration version: 1.3.0 author: Hermes Agent license: MIT metadata: hermes: tags: [image_gen, openrouter, workflow, flux, background-processing] related_skills: [openrouter-image-generation] --- # OpenRouter Image Generation Workflow This skill documents the complete approach for generating images via OpenRouter API with Flux.2 model, including background processing, error handling, and HTML integration. ## When to Use This Workflow Use this workflow when you need to generate images via OpenRouter API and integrate them into documents. This approach is particularly valuable for: - Generating **individual or series/trilogy book covers** with consistent typography - Chapter header illustrations for manuscripts - Batch image generation with progress tracking - Robust error handling and recovery - HTML document integration **Series/trilogy trigger:** When the user asks to "redo covers" or "regenerate covers" for a multi-book series (e.g., "redo the covers for books 1, 2, and 3"), load this skill and follow the Series/Trilogy Cover Pipeline section below. ## Key Components ### 1. Background Processing ```python # Run the script in the background to avoid blocking terminal(background=True, command="python /path/to/script.py > /tmp/log.txt 2>&1 &", notify_on_complete=True) ``` ### 2. API Request Functions #### Flux.2 (standard pattern) ```python def generate_image(prompt, output_path, api_key, model="black-forest-labs/flux.2-max"): """ Generate a single image and save to file. Handles API errors, timeouts, and file verification. """ url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions" headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {api_key}'} payload = { "model": model, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are an AI assistant that generates images."}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Generate an image:\\n\\n{prompt}\\n\\nReturn as base64 PNG."} ], "modalities": ["image"] } try: response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=120) response.raise_for_status() result = response.json() # Extract image data choices = result.get('choices', []) if not choices or 'message' not in choices[0]: raise ValueError("Invalid response structure") images = choices[0]['message'].get('images', []) if not images: raise ValueError("No images in response") img_data = images[0] if not isinstance(img_data, dict) or 'image_url' not in img_data: raise ValueError("Invalid image data") img_url = img_data['image_url'] if not isinstance(img_url, dict) or 'url' not in img_url: raise ValueError("No image URL provided") img_url_str = img_url['url'] if not img_url_str.startswith('data:image/png;base64,'): raise ValueError("Unexpected image format") # Decode and save img_b64 = img_url_str.split(',')[1] img_bytes = base64.b64decode(img_b64) with open(output_path, 'wb') as f: f.write(img_bytes) # Verify file exists if not Path(output_path).exists(): raise FileNotFoundError("Failed to save image file") return output_path except Exception as e: # Log error and return None for retry print(f"Error generating image: {e}") return None #### Gemini Flash Image (multimodal content format) Use this model (`google/gemini-2.5-flash-image`) via OpenRouter when you need higher-quality, photorealistic cover art. The payload format differs from Flux — it uses a structured content array rather than a plain string: ```python def generate_image_gemini(prompt, output_path, api_key, model="google/gemini-2.5-flash-image"): """Generate image using Gemini Flash Image via OpenRouter.""" url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions" headers = { "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}", "Content-Type": "application/json", "HTTP-Referer": "https://hermes.local", "X-Title": "Hermes Image Generation" } payload = { "model": model, "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": prompt} ] } ] } response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=180) response.raise_for_status() result = response.json() images = result["choices"][0]["message"].get("images", []) img_data = images[0] img_url = img_data["image_url"]["url"] if img_url.startswith("data:image/png;base64,"): b64 = img_url.split(",", 1)[1] img_bytes = base64.b64decode(b64) elif img_url.startswith("http"): img_resp = requests.get(img_url, timeout=60) img_bytes = img_resp.content with open(output_path, "wb") as f: f.write(img_bytes) return output_path ``` **Fallback strategy:** Try Gemini first for cover art (better composition and lighting). If it fails, fall back to Flux.2-max and retry as described in batch processing below. **Pitfalls:** - Gemini Flash Image only accepts the `content: [{type: "text", text: "..."}]` format — NOT the string-based content or `modalities` field that Flux uses. - Setting `modalities: ["image"]` on Gemini calls causes a 400 error. - Gemini may return square (1024×1024) images instead of portrait. Be prepared to extend the canvas (see Letterbox technique in Section 7). ### 3. Batch Processing with Progress Tracking ```python def generate_images_batch(prompts, output_dir, api_key, model="black-forest-labs/flux.2-max"): """ Generate multiple images with progress tracking and error recovery. Runs in background with notifications on completion. """ success_count = 0 fail_count = 0 failures = [] for name, prompt in prompts.items(): output_path = Path(output_dir) / f"{name}.png" # Generate image result = generate_image(prompt, str(output_path), api_key, model) if result: print(f"✅ Generated {name}") success_count += 1 else: print(f"❌ Failed to generate {name}") fail_count += 1 failures.append(name) # Delay to avoid rate limiting time.sleep(3) print(f"\nSummary: {success_count} succeeded, {fail_count} failed") if failures: print(f"Failed: {', '.join(failures)}") return success_count, fail_count, failures ``` ### 4. HTML Integration ```python def insert_images_into_html(html_path, image_dir, mapping): """ Insert generated images into HTML document. mapping: {placeholder_name: image_filename} """ with open(html_path, 'r') as f: html_content = f.read() for placeholder, image_file in mapping.items(): img_path = Path(image_dir) / image_file if not img_path.exists(): print(f"Warning: {image_file} not found") continue # Create img tag img_tag = f'' # Find insertion point using regex patterns if placeholder == 'cover': # Insert after cover-author div in cover section pattern = r'(
.*?)(
.*?
)' match = re.search(pattern, html_content, re.DOTALL) if match: new_content = match.group(1) + match.group(2) + '\n ' + img_tag + '\n
' html_content = html_content.replace(match.group(0), new_content) print(f"Inserted cover image") elif placeholder.startswith('chapter'): # Insert after chapter heading h3 tag chapter_num = placeholder.replace('chapter', '') heading = None if chapter_num == '1': heading = "The Builder's Blood" elif chapter_num == '2': heading = "The Navy Way" elif chapter_num == '4': heading = "The Garage Stays Open" elif chapter_num == '5': heading = "The TV Repair Shop" elif chapter_num == '6': heading = "The Engineering of Everything" elif chapter_num == '7': heading = "Chapter xx: Engineer vs. Executive" # Fallback else: heading = f"Chapter {chapter_num}" pattern = rf']*>{heading}' match = re.search(pattern, html_content) if match: new_content = html_content.replace( match.group(0), match.group(0) + '\n' + img_tag + '\n' ) html_content = new_content print(f"Inserted chapter {chapter_num} image") # Write modified HTML with open(html_path, 'w') as f: f.write(html_content) # Remove duplicate images if any cleanup_duplicate_images(html_path) ``` ### 5. Duplicate Cleanup ```python def cleanup_duplicate_images(html_path): """ Remove duplicate image tags that may have been inserted multiple times. """ with open(html_path, 'r') as f: html_content = f.read() # Find all cover image tags cover_img_pattern = r'' matches = list(re.finditer(cover_img_pattern, html_content)) if len(matches) > 1: # Keep only the first one after cover div cover_div_end = html_content.find('', html_content.find('
')) if cover_div_end != -1: # Find first cover img after cover div first_valid_img = None for match in matches: if match.start() > cover_div_end: first_valid_img = match break if first_valid_img: # Remove all others for match in matches: if match != first_valid_img: html_content = html_content.replace(match.group(0), '') print(f"Removed {len(matches)-1} duplicate cover images") # Write back with open(html_path, 'w') as f: f.write(html_content) ``` ## Lessons Learned from Trial and Error ### 1. API Response Structure - The image URL is deeply nested in the JSON response - Need to handle cases where fields might be missing - Base64 data URL requires stripping the prefix before decoding ### 2. Error Handling - API calls can fail for many reasons (network, rate limiting, model issues) - Always verify files are created successfully - Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for transient failures - Log errors with context for debugging ### 3. HTML Integration - Understanding the HTML structure is crucial for correct image placement - Use regex patterns that are specific enough but flexible - Handle cases where insertion points might not exist - Clean up duplicates from multiple insertion attempts - For files sent over Telegram or similar channels, prefer embedding the generated cover as a base64 `data:` URI so the HTML stays self-contained ### 4. Performance Considerations - Running in background prevents timeouts from blocking - Include delays between requests to avoid rate limiting - Verify file existence before proceeding - Use efficient string operations for HTML manipulation ### 5. Robustness - Always check if files exist before trying to read them - Handle different image formats gracefully - Provide meaningful error messages - Clean up temporary files if needed - If local config files are malformed YAML, extract the needed API key with a targeted regex instead of assuming the whole config can be parsed safely - **Sourcing API keys from .env:** When running in terminal sessions or cron jobs, environment variables from the agent's session may not propagate. Read the key directly from `~/.hermes/.env` as a fallback: ```python env_file = Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/.env")) api_key = os.environ.get("OPENROUTER_API_KEY") if not api_key and env_file.exists(): for line in open(env_file): if line.startswith("OPENROUTER_API_KEY=") and "***" not in line: api_key = line.split("=", 1)[1].strip().strip("'\"") ``` ### 6. Cover-Generation QA Loop - For premium cover art, one generation is often not enough - After generating a candidate, run vision QA to assess: negative space for title/author, absence of baked-in gibberish text, clutter level, and whether the image reads as a real cover instead of generic concept art - If the image is too busy, regenerate with stricter prompt constraints such as: `leave generous negative space`, `no logos/text/symbols`, `avoid clutter`, and `main subject in middle band` - This iterative generate → critique → regenerate loop produces materially better book-cover results than accepting the first image ### Google Gemini Direct API (when OpenRouter is unavailable) When OpenRouter's Gemini endpoint is unreachable or you need direct Google API access, use Google's own Gemini API directly. The key is stored as `GOOGLE_AI_STUDIO_KEY` in `~/.hermes/.env` and must be sourced via bash: ```python import subprocess, requests, json, base64 # Source the key from .env (it's NOT in os.environ by default) result = subprocess.run( ["bash", "-c", "source ~/.hermes/.env && echo $GOOGLE_AI_STUDIO_KEY"], capture_output=True, text=True ) api_key = result.stdout.strip() # Direct Gemini API endpoint url = f"https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/gemini-2.5-flash-image:generateContent?key={api_key}" payload = { "contents": [{ "parts": [{"text": "Your image prompt here. Leave top 40% empty. 3:4 portrait."}] }], "generationConfig": {"temperature": 1.0} } response = requests.post(url, json=payload, timeout=90) data = response.json() candidate = data.get('candidates', [{}])[0] parts = candidate.get('content', {}).get('parts', []) for part in parts: if 'inlineData' in part: img_bytes = base64.b64decode(part['inlineData']['data']) with open("output.png", "wb") as f: f.write(img_bytes) ``` **Key differences from OpenRouter pattern:** - NO `modalities` field — Gemini doesn't accept it - NO `Authorization` header — key is in URL query parameter - Response uses `candidates[0].content.parts[].inlineData` NOT `choices[0].message.images` - Returns PNG bytes directly (base64), not a JSON image URL - Often returns square (1024×1024) images — plan for canvas extension ### 6.5 Pre-Typography Canvas Adjustment (Generate → QA → Extend → Text) Do NOT blindly regenerate when the raw image has good art but poor composition. Instead, use a **two-pass QA approach**: **Pass 1 — Assess the raw image:** 1. Generate the raw image (no text, no overlays) 2. Run vision QA asking specifically about: - Does the top 40% have enough clean negative space for stacked title text? - Does the bottom 15% have clean space for the author name? - What's the actual image size and aspect ratio? (Gemini often returns 1024×1024 squares) - Is the subject positioned too high/low/off-center for a book cover layout? 3. Based on QA feedback, decide: regenerate with a better prompt OR extend the canvas **Canvas extension (preferred when art quality is good but composition is off):** - If the Earth/planet is too high → add 60% of extra height to the top, 40% to bottom - If the subject is centered but the image is square → extend both top AND bottom evenly - If the subject is too low → add more to the bottom, less to the top - **Never extend less than 200px at top** — the title zone needs at least 200-300px of pure black for a 2-5 word stacked title at 52-58pt - Always resize to **1024×1536 (2:3)** — standard book cover ratio **Pass 2 — Add typography onto the adjusted canvas:** - Once the canvas has clean black letterbox zones, add typography on top - Text on pure black needs only a 1px shadow, NO background boxes - Run a second vision QA to verify text placement ### 7. Cover Typography and Branding (Final Polish) When generating retail-ready book covers, follow these specific design standards for professional consistency: - **Typography Specifications:** Users often require specific typography (e.g., "30pt white title, one word per line, stacked"). For 1024x1536 covers, "30pt" typically translates to approximately 40 pixels in height, and "16pt" translates to 21-22 pixels. - **Transparency for Visibility:** To ensure background art is not "occluded" (blocked), use semi-transparent black boxes (e.g., `fill=(0,0,0,120)` in PIL) rather than solid black bars. - **Vertical Title Stacking:** For long titles or specific aesthetic requirements, stack words vertically (one word per line). This maximizes the "action zone" of the background art and prevent cutoff. - **Even Spacing Calculation:** Calculate line heights and start position mathematically to center the stacked text vertically within the title zone: ```python line_h = int(title_font_size * 1.2) # consistent inter-word spacing total_title_h = line_h * len(title_words) # total height of stacked title title_zone_h = int(target_h * 0.35) # title occupies top 35% of canvas title_start_y = (title_zone_h - total_title_h) // 2 # center within zone ``` This ensures mathematically equal spacing between every word, avoiding the "cramped at top, loose at bottom" look of hardcoded offsets. - **Author Placement:** Center the author name horizontally at the bottom of the cover (e.g., `h - 160` for a 1536px height). - **Canvas Extension (Letterbox Technique):** When the AI-generated image lacks enough negative space at the top (e.g., Earth/planet is too high), add pure black bars by extending the canvas rather than re-generating: ```python from PIL import Image target_w, target_h = 1024, 1536 # 2:3 book cover ratio img = Image.open(input_path) orig_w, orig_h = img.size ratio = target_w / orig_w img_resized = img.resize((target_w, int(orig_h * ratio)), Image.LANCZOS) extra_h = target_h - img_resized.size[1] top_extend = int(extra_h * 0.6) # 60% to top, 40% to bottom bottom_extend = extra_h - top_extend canvas = Image.new("RGB", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0)) canvas.paste(img_resized, (0, top_extend)) ``` This creates clean black letterbox zones for the title (top) and author (bottom) with zero risk of text overlapping artwork. - **Full-Bleed Crop (alternative to letterbox):** When the AI image is square (1024×1024) and the center has valuable art, scale it up to fill the portrait height and crop the sides instead of adding black bars. This eliminates white sidebars and gives a professional full-bleed look: ```python target_w, target_h = 1024, 1536 img = Image.open(input_path) scale_h = target_h / img.size[1] # e.g. 1536/1024 = 1.5 img_scaled = img.resize((int(img.size[0] * scale_h), target_h), Image.LANCZOS) x_offset = (img_scaled.size[0] - target_w) // 2 # center-crop width canvas = img_scaled.crop((x_offset, 0, x_offset + target_w, target_h)) ``` **When to use which:** Letterbox (black bars) when the art has important content at the very edges that shouldn't be cropped. Full-bleed crop when the art is centered and the edges are uniform (sky, ground, space) — this looks more professional and avoids the "boxed-in" appearance. - **Gradient Overlay for Busy Backgrounds:** When the artwork has bright elements that reduce text legibility (e.g., a glowing cave opening, a lit planet, a bright horizon), use a subtle dark gradient at the top and/or bottom of the image rather than solid black bars or opaque boxes: ```python overlay = Image.new("RGBA", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0, 0)) draw = ImageDraw.Draw(overlay) # Top gradient (progressive dark fade) grad_height = int(target_h * 0.28) # fade from ~0 to 28% of cover height for y in range(grad_height): alpha = int(100 * (1 - y / grad_height)) if alpha > 0: draw.rectangle([0, y, target_w, y+1], fill=(0, 0, 0, min(alpha, 70))) # Bottom gradient (for author name readability) bot_grad = int(target_h * 0.10) # bottom 10% for y in range(bot_grad): alpha = int(80 * (y / bot_grad)) if alpha > 0: draw.rectangle([0, target_h - bot_grad + y, target_w, target_h - bot_grad + y + 1], fill=(0, 0, 0, min(alpha, 60))) ``` This preserves the artwork underneath while ensuring text remains readable. Works best in combination with a subtle 2px text shadow. - **Inch-Based and Percentage Font Adjustments:** After initial QA, users often request specific positioning or sizing tweaks. Handle these with math: - **"1.5 inches from the top":** At standard book cover resolution (1024×1536 ≈ 170-200 DPI for a 6×9 book), 1.5 inches ≈ 255-300 pixels. Calculate: `margin_px = int(1.5 * (target_h / 9))` where 9 is the cover height in inches. ```python # For a 6×9 cover at 1024×1536: dpi = target_h / 9 # ~170 DPI title_top_margin = int(1.5 * dpi) # ~256px from top edge ``` - **"Increase font size by X%":** Multiply the current size and round to nearest integer: `new_size = int(old_size * 1.30)` for a 30% increase. Apply to both title and author font sizes consistently. - **Multi-round iteration pattern:** When the user gives successive positioning/sizing feedback, keep a single Python script and patch individual parameters (title_start_y, font_size, top_extend_ratio) rather than rewriting from scratch. Re-run only the affected book after each change. - **Per-book canvas ratios:** Different books in a series may need different top extension ratios (0.60-0.75). Document the per-book ratio in a dict alongside the font specs so the typography script stays DRY. - **Text Rendering with Shadow:** For pure black letterbox zones, no background box is needed — just drop a subtle 1px shadow for polish. When text must sit on the art itself, use semi-transparent boxes instead. - **Post-Typography Vision QA:** After overlaying text, run a second vision QA pass specifically asking about: - Text legibility and overlap with artwork - Consistent vertical spacing between stacked words - Equivalent font sizes for title vs author - Margin bleed safety (stay 5-10% from edges) If QA flags issues, correct the script and re-run before declaring the cover done. #### Selection rule of thumb For sci-fi covers, prefer the candidate with: 1. strongest title-space contrast, 2. clearest sense of scale/civilization, 3. no embedded text/watermarks, 4. recognizable transportation corridors/roads, 5. minimal visual clutter in the title zone. ## Series/Trilogy Cover Pipeline When the user asks to "redo the covers" for a multi-book series (e.g., a 3-book trilogy), follow this end-to-end pipeline to produce N coordinated covers with consistent typography and then hand off to the publishing package builder. ### Pipeline Steps **Step 1 — Plan the series prompts** Write one prompt per book. Each prompt must share a consistent structure: - Same aspect ratio requirement (2:3 portrait, 1024×1536) - Same negative space constraints (top 40% clean for title, bottom 15% clean for author) - Same "no text/logos/watermarks" rule - Different subject/scene per book that advances the series visually Example (sci-fi trilogy): ``` Book 1 (First Generation): Mars canyon city — domes in a deep canyon, red dusty landscape Book 2 (Second Generation): Lava tube habitat — underground colony, warm glow, mineral walls Book 3 (Third Generation): Alien hive ship — mysterious bioluminescent ship, deep space ``` Run the prompts in a single Python script with `notify_on_complete=True` to batch-generate all N backgrounds in sequence. Include `time.sleep(3)` between generations to avoid rate limits. **Step 2 — QA each raw image** After all backgrounds are generated, run vision_analyze on each one, asking specifically: - Is the top 40% clean enough for stacked white title text? - Is the bottom 15% clean for the author name? - Are there any embedded text, watermarks, or digital artifacts? - Is the aspect ratio suitable (square needs canvas extension)? Note which books need canvas adjustments vs. which are ready. **Step 3 — Apply consistent typography across the series** Write a single Python script that processes all N images. The script must: - Use the SAME font path for all books (DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf or LiberationSans-Bold.ttf) - Use the SAME typography rules (font size may vary by word count, but style is identical) - Use the SAME author name placement - Extend square (1024×1024) images to portrait (1024×1536) with black bars (60-75% top, 25-40% bottom) **Define per-book parameters in a dict** so adjustments are data-driven: ```python books = { "First_Generation": { "title_words": ["FIRST", "GENERATION"], "title_size": 58, "top_extend_ratio": 0.70, # more top room if subject is high }, "Second_Generation": { "title_words": ["SECOND", "GENERATION"], "title_size": 52, "top_extend_ratio": 0.68, "add_top_gradient": True, # if bright elements in title zone }, } ``` This makes it easy to tweak one book without touching the others. Per-book adjustments: - If a book's subject is too high (top 40% cluttered), increase the top extension ratio (e.g., 0.75 instead of 0.60) - If a bright light source sits in the title zone, add a subtle dark gradient overlay (alpha 0-80 over the first 50-100px of art) - Ensure every word of the stacked title ends before the artwork begins — verify mathematically: `word_y + text_height_approx < art_start_y` **Step 4 — QA each final cover** Run vision_analyze on each finished cover asking about: - Text legibility and overlap with artwork - Consistent vertical spacing between stacked words - Any text overlapping the artwork boundary - If any issues are found, fix the script and re-run only that book **Step 5 — Hand off to package builder** Once all N covers pass QA, tell the user the covers are ready and then either: - If this is for an existing package, patch `manuscript-preparation-and-delivery` to rebuild the zip - If this is a new package, build a series/trilogy package structure (see manuscript-preparation-and-delivery skill) ### Common Pitfalls - **Inconsistent prompt structure** — Always include "leave generous negative space at top 40%" in every prompt. The AI will default to centering the subject if you don't. - **Square output from Gemini** — Gemini Flash Image often returns 1024×1024 squares regardless of prompt. Always plan for canvas extension. - **Not checking overlap** — After typography, always verify the last word of the stacked title doesn't overlap the artwork. If it does, increase the top extension ratio. - **Batch failures** — If one book's generation fails, don't restart the whole batch. Just regenerate that one book. ## When This Approach Works Well - **Batch image generation**: Perfect for generating multiple images with different prompts - **HTML integration**: Seamlessly integrates generated images into existing HTML documents - **Error recovery**: Handles failures gracefully and continues processing - **Progress tracking**: Provides clear feedback on success/failure rates ## Limitations - **API dependent**: Requires OpenRouter API access and a valid API key - **Model specific**: Uses Flux.2 model; may need adjustments for other models - **HTML structure dependent**: Requires understanding of target HTML structure - **Rate limits**: Subject to OpenRouter's rate limits ## Memoir Cover Prompts See `references/memoir-cover-prompts.md` for domain-specific prompt templates and typography settings that worked for Bob's memoirs. Covers genre-specific visual metaphor patterns (electrical-spark-to-stars, cabin/light nostalgia), canvas extension workflows, and gradient overlay recipes for memoir covers. Also see: - `references/memoir-cover-prompts.md` — domain-specific prompt templates and typography settings for Bob's memoirs. - `references/book-cover-design-recipes.md` — quadrant/radial layout technique and bold typography overlapping artwork. - `references/gradient-overlay-cover-typography.md` — alternative cover typography approach using gradient darkening + shadowed white text instead of letterbox bars. Best when artwork should show through behind text. Includes the "80% width title scaling" technique and per-book parameter dict pattern. ## Best Practices 1. **Test with a single image first** before batch processing 2. **Include proper error handling** for all API interactions 3. **Verify file creation** after each generation 4. **Use appropriate delays** between requests to avoid rate limiting 5. **Clean up duplicates** if running multiple times 6. **Monitor progress** and log errors for debugging ## Related Skills - `openrouter-image-generation` (basic skill) - `html-integration` (for HTML manipulation) - `background-processing` (for running tasks asynchronously) ", "path": "openrouter-image-generation-workflow/SKILL.md", "skill_dir": "/home/bob/.hermes/skills/openrouter-image-generation-workflow", "linked_files": {"references": ["references/gradient-overlay-cover-typography.md", "references/memoir-cover-prompts.md", "references/book-cover-design-recipes.md"]}, "usage_hint": "To view linked files, call skill_view(name, file_path) where file_path is e.g. 'references/api.md' or 'assets/config.yaml'", "required_environment_variables": [], "required_commands": [], "missing_required_environment_variables": [], "missing_credential_files": [], "missing_required_commands": [], "setup_needed": false, "setup_skipped": false, "readiness_status": "available", "metadata": {"hermes": {"tags": ["image_gen", "openrouter", "workflow", "flux", "background-processing"], "related_skills": ["openrouter-image-generation"]}}}

- You want a professional "text-over-artwork" look rather than black bars

## Technique

### Step 1: Add gradient overlays

```python
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageEnhance, ImageFont

img = Image.open(raw_path).convert("RGBA")
w, h = img.size

overlay = Image.new("RGBA", (w, h), (0, 0, 0, 0))
draw_overlay = ImageDraw.Draw(overlay)

# Top gradient for title zone (darker, ~35% of height)
grad_height_top = int(h * 0.35)
for y in range(grad_height_top):
    alpha = int(180 * (1 - y / grad_height_top))
    draw_overlay.rectangle([0, y, w, y+1], fill=(0, 0, 0, min(alpha, 140)))

# Bottom gradient for author zone (~15% of height)
grad_height_bot = int(h * 0.15)
for y in range(grad_height_bot):
    alpha = int(140 * (y / grad_height_bot))
    draw_overlay.rectangle([0, h - grad_height_bot + y, w, h - grad_height_bot + y + 1], 
                          fill=(0, 0, 0, min(alpha, 100)))

img = Image.alpha_composite(img, overlay).convert("RGB")
```

### Step 2: Add shadowed typography

```python
draw = ImageDraw.Draw(img)

# Title font sizing: scale to ~80% of cover width
font_size = 60
font = ImageFont.truetype("/usr/share/fonts/truetype/liberation/LiberationSans-Bold.ttf", font_size)

# Get max line width and scale
lines = title_text.split('\n')  # e.g. ["THE", "OXYGEN", "GAMBLE"]
max_line_w = max(draw.textbbox((0,0), l, font=font)[2] - draw.textbbox((0,0), l, font=font)[0] for l in lines)
target_w_px = int(w * 0.8)
scale = target_w_px / max_line_w if max_line_w > 0 else 1
adjusted_size = max(40, min(90, int(font_size * scale)))
title_font = ImageFont.truetype(font_path, adjusted_size)

# Draw centered stacked title
title_y = int(h * 0.03)
for line in lines:
    bbox = draw.textbbox((0, 0), line, font=title_font)
    lw = bbox[2] - bbox[0]
    lh = bbox[3] - bbox[1]
    x = (w - lw) // 2
    
    # Shadow for legibility over art
    draw.text((x+2, title_y+2), line, font=title_font, fill=(0,0,0,180))
    draw.text((x, title_y), line, font=title_font, fill=(255,255,255,255))
    
    title_y += lh + 5

# Author name at bottom with dark box
author_text = "Bob J Mills"
author_font_size = 32
author_font = ImageFont.truetype(font_path, author_font_size)
ab = draw.textbbox((0, 0), author_text, font=author_font)
ax = (w - (ab[2] - ab[0])) // 2
ay = h - int(h * 0.08)
box_h = int(h * 0.08)
draw.rectangle([0, h - box_h - 10, w, h], fill=(0, 0, 0, 160))
draw.text((ax+2, ay+2), author_text, font=author_font, fill=(0,0,0,180))
draw.text((ax, ay), author_text, font=author_font, fill=(255,255,255,255))
```

Add a small series + book number line at the very top:

```python
sub_font = ImageFont.truetype(font_path, 16)
series_text = "The Lunar Foundation  •  Book 2"
sb = draw.textbbox((0, 0), series_text, font=sub_font)
sub_x = (w - (sb[2] - sb[0])) // 2
sub_y = int(h * 0.01)
draw.text((sub_x+1, sub_y+1), series_text, font=sub_font, fill=(0,0,0,160))
draw.text((sub_x, sub_y), series_text, font=sub_font, fill=(200,200,200,255))
```

## Comparison with Letterbox Approach

| Factor | Gradient Overlay | Letterbox (Black Bars) |
|--------|-----------------|----------------------|
| Artwork visibility | Art shows through behind text | Art completely hidden under bars |
| Text legibility | Good but varies with art brightness | Excellent (pure black behind white text) |
| Professional look | Modern, integrated | Clean, traditional cover |
| Best for | Dark/moody artwork with good contrast | Bright/busy artwork |
| Shadow needed | 2px shadow essential | 1px shadow sufficient |

{"content": "#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Regenerate all No Blue Sky covers — original art, best-selling sci-fi inspired style, correct typography."""
import base64, json, os, subprocess, time
from pathlib import Path
import requests
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFont, ImageEnhance

OUTPUT_DIR = Path("/home/bob/books/publishing_output/covers")

# Get API key
result = subprocess.run(
    ["bash", "-c", "source ~/.hermes/.env && echo $GOOGLE_AI_STUDIO_KEY"],
    capture_output=True, text=True
)
api_key = result.stdout.strip()

BOOKS = [
    {
        "num": 1,
        "title_words": ["BUILT", "FROM", "DUST"],
        "prompt": (
            "Book cover artwork for a sci-fi novel. A vast Martian colony under construction — "
            "half-finished geodesic domes rise from the red dust landscape. Massive construction cranes "
            "and machinery silhouette against a dusty orange sky. A tiny Earth hangs in the distance. "
            "Cinematic widescreen composition, dramatic lighting, sense of human endeavor against an alien world. "
            "Colors: deep Martian red, warm orange, silver metal, pale blue Earth. "
            "Leave the top 40% of the image as clean, empty negative space (dusty sky gradient) "
            "for title text placement. Leave the bottom 15% clean for author name. "
            "CRITICAL: No text, no watermarks, no letters, no logos anywhere. "
            "Inspired by best-selling sci-fi cover aesthetics but completely original — no copied elements."
        )
    },
    {
        "num": 2,
        "title_words": ["THE", "OXYGEN", "GAMBLE"],
        "prompt": (
            "Book cover artwork for a sci-fi novel. A massive oxygen processing facility on Mars — "
            "towering silver tanks and intricate pipe networks stretch across the red landscape. "
            "Vapor clouds vent from pressure valves, catching the harsh sunlight. A dark dust storm "
            "looms on the horizon. High contrast, dramatic industrial sci-fi. "
            "Colors: silver metal, rust red, white vapor clouds, deep storm-darkened sky. "
            "Leave the top 40% of the image as clean, empty negative space (storm sky gradient) "
            "for title text placement. Leave the bottom 15% clean for author name. "
            "CRITICAL: No text, no watermarks, no letters, no logos anywhere. "
            "Inspired by best-selling sci-fi cover aesthetics but completely original — no copied elements."
        )
    },
    {
        "num": 3,
        "title_words": ["RIVERS", "UNDER", "MARS"],
        "prompt": (
            "Book cover artwork for a sci-fi novel. A vast underground cavern beneath Mars — "
            "crystal-clear blue water rivers winding through ancient rock, illuminated by bioluminescent "
            "algae and mining lights. A small drilling platform stands on a rock outcropping above the water. "
            "The cavern ceiling glitters with mineral deposits. Magical, discovery-filled atmosphere. "
            "Colors: luminous aqua blue, warm amber lights, dark basalt rock, silver equipment. "
            "Leave the top 40% of the image as clean, empty negative space (dark cavern ceiling gradient) "
            "for title text placement. Leave the bottom 15% clean for author name. "
            "CRITICAL: No text, no watermarks, no letters, no logos anywhere. "
            "Inspired by best-selling sci-fi cover aesthetics but completely original — no copied elements."
        )
    },
    {
        "num": 4,
        "title_words": ["RED", "CHARTER"],
        "prompt": (
            "Book cover artwork for a sci-fi novel. The grand government plaza of a Martian colony — "
            "a sweeping curved building with tall columns under a massive transparent dome. A red flag "
            "with a geometric symbol flies prominently. Colonists in practical Mars suits gather in the "
            "square below. Warm golden sunset light filters through the dome. Political, aspirational, grand. "
            "Colors: Martian red, warm gold, silver dome framework, deep indigo sky beyond the dome. "
            "Leave the top 40% of the image as clean, empty negative space (dome ceiling gradient) "
            "for title text placement. Leave the bottom 15% clean for author name. "
            "CRITICAL: No text, no watermarks, no letters, no logos anywhere. "
            "Inspired by best-selling sci-fi cover aesthetics but completely original — no copied elements."
        )
    },
    {
        "num": 5,
        "title_words": ["FIRST", "MARTIAN", "NATION"],
        "prompt": (
            "Book cover artwork for a sci-fi novel. A triumphant celebration on Mars — multiple illuminated "
            "domes spread across a terraformed valley, rockets launching in the distance with bright exhaust trails. "
            "In the foreground, a large Martian flag (red with a silver planetary symbol) waves on a pole. "
            "The sky transitions from dusty orange at the horizon to deep space black above. Hopeful, epic, monumental. "
            "Colors: bright red, warm gold, silver, orange sunset, deep space black with scattered faint stars. "
            "Leave the top 40% of the image as clean, empty negative space (sky gradient) "
            "for title text placement. Leave the bottom 15% clean for author name. "
            "CRITICAL: No text, no watermarks, no letters, no logos anywhere. "
            "Inspired by best-selling sci-fi cover aesthetics but completely original — no copied elements."
        )
    }
]

def generate_artwork(book):
    """Generate artwork for one book."""
    raw_out = str(OUTPUT_DIR / f"NBS_{book['num']}_Built_from_Dust_raw.png" if book['num'] == 1 else 
                  OUTPUT_DIR / f"NBS_{book['num']}_{'_'.join(book['title_words'])}_raw.png")
    
    # Fix book 1 naming
    if book['num'] == 1:
        raw_out = str(OUTPUT_DIR / "NBS_1_Built_from_Dust_raw.png")
    elif book['num'] == 2:
        raw_out = str(OUTPUT_DIR / "NBS_2_Oxygen_Gamble_raw.png")
    elif book['num'] == 3:
        raw_out = str(OUTPUT_DIR / "NBS_3_Rivers_Under_Mars_raw.png")
    elif book['num'] == 4:
        raw_out = str(OUTPUT_DIR / "NBS_4_Red_Charter_raw.png")
    elif book['num'] == 5:
        raw_out = str(OUTPUT_DIR / "NBS_5_First_Martian_Nation_raw.png")
    
    print(f"\n{'='*60}")
    print(f"Generating: {' '.join(book['title_words'])} (Book {book['num']})")
    
    url = f"https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/gemini-2.5-flash-image:generateContent?key={api_key}"
    payload = {
        "contents": [{"parts": [{"text": book['prompt']}]}],
        "generationConfig": {"temperature": 1.0}
    }
    
    resp = requests.post(url, json=payload, timeout=120)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    data = resp.json()
    
    candidate = data.get('candidates', [{}])[0]
    parts = candidate.get('content', {}).get('parts', [])
    
    for part in parts:
        if isinstance(part, dict) and 'inlineData' in part:
            img_bytes = base64.b64decode(part['inlineData']['data'])
            with open(raw_out, "wb") as f:
                f.write(img_bytes)
            print(f"  ✅ Saved raw: {Path(raw_out).name} ({len(img_bytes)//1024}KB)")
            return raw_out
    
    print(f"  ❌ No image data in response")
    print(f"  DEBUG: {json.dumps(data, indent=2)[:300]}")
    return None

def apply_typography(book, raw_path):
    """Apply typography overlay to create final cover."""
    if not raw_path or not os.path.exists(raw_path):
        print(f"  ❌ Raw file missing: {raw_path}")
        return
    
    target_w, target_h = 1200, 1800
    
    # Map raw to final output
    name_map = {
        1: "NBS_1_Built_from_Dust_Cover.png",
        2: "NBS_2_Oxygen_Gamble_Cover.png",
        3: "NBS_3_Rivers_Under_Mars_Cover.png",
        4: "NBS_4_Red_Charter_Cover.png",
        5: "NBS_5_First_Martian_Nation_Cover.png",
    }
    final_out = str(OUTPUT_DIR / name_map[book['num']])
    
    print(f"  Applying typography to {Path(raw_path).name}...")
    
    img = Image.open(raw_path).convert("RGBA")
    w, h = img.size
    
    # Scale to portrait
    scale = target_h / h
    new_w = int(w * scale)
    img = img.resize((new_w, target_h), Image.LANCZOS)
    
    if new_w > target_w:
        xo = (new_w - target_w) // 2
        img = img.crop((xo, 0, xo + target_w, target_h))
    else:
        canvas = Image.new("RGBA", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0, 255))
        canvas.paste(img, ((target_w - new_w) // 2, 0))
        img = canvas
    
    # Brighten & contrast
    img = ImageEnhance.Brightness(img).enhance(1.20)
    img = ImageEnhance.Contrast(img).enhance(1.1)
    
    # Gradient overlay
    overlay = Image.new("RGBA", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0, 0))
    dover = ImageDraw.Draw(overlay)
    
    for y in range(int(target_h * 0.30)):
        a = int(120 * (1 - y / (target_h * 0.30)))
        dover.rectangle([0, y, target_w, y+1], fill=(0, 0, 0, min(a, 90)))
    for y in range(int(target_h * 0.15)):
        a = int(100 * (y / (target_h * 0.15)))
        dover.rectangle([0, target_h - int(target_h * 0.15) + y, target_w, target_h - int(target_h * 0.15) + y + 1],
                       fill=(0, 0, 0, min(a, 80)))
    
    img = Image.alpha_composite(img, overlay).convert("RGB")
    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(img)
    font_path = "/usr/share/fonts/truetype/liberation/LiberationSans-Bold.ttf"
    
    # --- TITLE (stacked words) ---
    title_words = book['title_words']
    
    # Find largest font that fits the widest word within 80% of cover width
    for test_size in range(300, 40, -2):
        font = ImageFont.truetype(font_path, test_size)
        max_w = max(draw.textbbox((0, 0), w, font=font)[2] - draw.textbbox((0, 0), w, font=font)[0] for w in title_words)
        if max_w <= int(target_w * 0.80):
            title_font_size = test_size
            break
    else:
        title_font_size = 40
    
    title_font = ImageFont.truetype(font_path, title_font_size)
    
    # Calculate line dimensions
    line_hs = []
    line_ws = []
    for word in title_words:
        bb = draw.textbbox((0, 0), word, font=title_font)
        line_ws.append(bb[2] - bb[0])
        line_hs.append(bb[3] - bb[1])
    
    line_gap = int(title_font_size * 0.12)
    total_stack_h = sum(line_hs) + line_gap * (len(title_words) - 1)
    
    # Center stacked title vertically in top 35% of cover
    title_zone_h = int(target_h * 0.35)
    start_y = (title_zone_h - total_stack_h) // 2 + int(target_h * 0.02)
    
    current_y = start_y
    for i, word in enumerate(title_words):
        x = (target_w - line_ws[i]) // 2
        for ox, oy in [(3, 3), (2, 2), (1, 1)]:
            draw.text((x+ox, current_y+oy), word, font=title_font, fill=(0, 0, 0, 180))
        draw.text((x, current_y), word, font=title_font, fill=(255, 255, 255, 255))
        current_y += line_hs[i] + line_gap
    
    max_word_pct = max(line_ws) / target_w * 100
    print(f"    Title: {' | '.join(title_words)} at {title_font_size}px ({max_word_pct:.0f}% widest)")
    
    # --- SERIES ---
    sf = ImageFont.truetype(font_path, 18)
    st = f"NO BLUE SKY  •  BOOK {book['num']}"
    sb = draw.textbbox((0, 0), st, font=sf)
    sx = (target_w - (sb[2] - sb[0])) // 2
    draw.text((sx+1, 9+1), st, font=sf, fill=(0, 0, 0, 160))
    draw.text((sx, 9), st, font=sf, fill=(200, 200, 200, 255))
    
    # --- AUTHOR ---
    author_text = "Bob J Mills"
    af = ImageFont.truetype(font_path, 100)
    ab = draw.textbbox((0, 0), author_text, font=af)
    aw = ab[2] - ab[0]
    ax = (target_w - aw) // 2
    ay = target_h - int(target_h * 0.07)
    
    bar_h = int(target_h * 0.09)
    draw.rectangle([0, target_h - bar_h - 5, target_w, target_h], fill=(0, 0, 0, 160))
    for ox, oy in [(2, 2), (1, 1)]:
        draw.text((ax+ox, ay+oy), author_text, font=af, fill=(0, 0, 0, 180))
    draw.text((ax, ay), author_text, font=af, fill=(255, 255, 255, 255))
    print(f"    Author: {author_text} at 100px ({aw}px)")
    
    img.save(final_out, quality=95)
    print(f"  ✅ Saved final: {Path(final_out).name}")
    return final_out

# === MAIN ===
print("="*60)
print("REGENERATING ALL NO BLUE SKY COVERS")
print("="*60)

for book in BOOKS:
    raw = generate_artwork(book)
    if raw:
        time.sleep(3)  # Rate limit between generations
        apply_typography(book, raw)
    else:
        print(f"  ⏭ Skipping typography for Book {book['num']} (no raw image)")

print("\n" + "="*60)
print("✅ ALL NO BLUE SKY COVERS COMPLETE")
print("="*60)
", "path": "/tmp/nbs_covers.py"}

The workflow differs from non-fiction chapter insertion because memoirs use organic transitions rather than numbered headers. #### When to Use - User says "add this new section to the end of the book" - A markdown file containing a final section (e.g., "The Future After Bob") needs to be appended after the existing ending - The manuscript uses narrative headers like `# Part One:`, `## Chapter One:`, or `### Transition:` markers rather than `# Chapter N:` numbered headers - The existing ending (epilogue, final chapter) must be preserved, not removed #### Step 1: Identify the Endpoint The manuscript's final substantive line is the natural anchor. Find it by searching for the last narrative paragraph, not the last line of the file (which may contain AI artifacts or old epilogues). In a memoir, the ending is often a reflective closing image — e.g., "the willingness to touch the outlet anyway" or "That is enough." ```python # Find the last meaningful line in the manuscript last_line_marker = "willingness to touch the outlet anyway" if last_line_marker in manuscript: idx = manuscript.rfind(last_line_marker) end_idx = manuscript.find('\\n', idx) if end_idx == -1: end_idx = len(manuscript) main_body = manuscript[:end_idx].strip() ``` #### Step 2: Write a Transitional Bridge Write 1-3 paragraphs in the author's established voice that bridge the existing ending into the new section. The transition should: - Return to a concrete present-moment scene (dinner, workshop, family) - Expand outward thematically to the larger question the new section addresses - Explicitly frame the new section (e.g., "One more story. Not a look backward — a look forward.") - Use the same tone, rhythm, and narrative style as the main manuscript ```markdown --- ## The Threshold Bob closes the document. Cindy is calling from downstairs. Dinner is on the table. The evening stretches ahead — ordinary, precious, irreplaceable. But a story this size does not end at a dinner table... What follows is not Bob's memory. It is Bob's imagination — offered to the generations who will inherit what he could only dream of building. --- ``` #### Step 3: Append Without Removing Anything Combine the three parts: ```python manuscript = main_body + "\\n\\n" + transition + "\\n\\n" + new_section ``` Do NOT remove the epilogue, AI artifacts, author's notes, or any other content. The existing ending is the user's work. Only insert the transition after it. #### Step 4: Build the TOC from Organic Headers Memoirs often use varied header styles. Parse multiple patterns: ```python toc_entries = [] for line in manuscript.split('\\n'): s = line.strip() m1 = re.match(r'^# (Part \\w+: .+)$', s) # Part headers if m1: toc_entries.append(('part', m1.group(1))); continue m2 = re.match(r'^## (Chapter \\w+: .+)$', s) # Chapter headers (Roman numerals) if m2: toc_entries.append(('chapter', m2.group(1))); continue if s == '# Epilogue: The Unwritten Future': toc_entries.append(('epilogue', s[2:].strip())); continue # Add the new final section toc_entries.append(('final', 'Final Section: The Future After Bob')) # Add ## subsections from the new section as sub-entries for line in new_section.split('\\n'): s = line.strip() m = re.match(r'^## (.+)$', s) if m and m.group(1) in known_subsections: toc_entries.append(('sub', m.group(1))) ``` #### Step 5: CSS for Memoir vs Non-Fiction Fiction/memoir uses indented paragraphs; non-fiction uses block paragraphs: ```css /* Memoir */ .chapter-content p { text-indent: 1.5em; } /* Non-fiction override for final section if it uses block style */ .final-section-content p { text-indent: 0; margin: 8px 0; } ``` #### Pitfalls - **Splitting on the wrong marker** — The manuscript may have `# Chapter` lines in its TOC that look like section headers. Always anchor your search to the last narrative paragraph, not regex-based chapter detection. - **Removing content accidentally** — The user explicitly said "do not remove content." Append only. Do not strip the epilogue, old transitions, or author notes even if they look like AI artifacts. - **Header style mismatch** — Memoirs may use `## Chapter One:` (Roman) while the user's build script expects `## Chapter 1:` (Arabic). Parse both patterns. - **New section headers conflicting with existing** — The new section's `##` sub-headings (e.g., "The Empty Chair") should appear in the TOC but NOT be treated as top-level chapters. Use a "sub" CSS class with indentation. - **Transition voice mismatch** — The bridge paragraph must match the manuscript's voice. For memoirs, this means first-person reflective, with concrete sensory details (smells, sounds, gestures). ### 4. minimum 1000px on shortest side, 2560px on longest recommended; quality 95) - [ ] AI Disclosure record (markdown file for reference) - [ ] Marketing copy with description, categories, and keywords ready to paste - [ ] ISBN for print version (if applicable) - [ ] Pricing strategy (royalty path, list price, territorial rights) ## Best Practices ### Content Creation - Write transitions that connect emotionally with readers - Balance action with introspection in fiction works - Show, don't tell - use sensory details and specific examples - Maintain consistent voice throughout the book ### Technical Implementation - Test PDF conversion early and often with sample chapters - Keep original AI prompts for future image regeneration - Maintain version control for all manuscript iterations - Create backup copies of all generated files ## Example Project Structure ``` book-project/ ├── manuscript/ │ ├── edited/ # Edited manuscript │ └── final.md # Final Markdown ├── formatting/ │ ├── html/ # HTML files │ └── css/ # CSS stylesheets ├── images/ │ ├── generated/ # AI-generated images │ └── final/ # Optimized images ├── pdf/ │ ├── drafts/ # Test PDFs │ └── final/ # Production PDFs └── scripts/ # Automation scripts ``` ## Integrated Single-Script Pipeline For production efficiency, build a single `generate_all.py` script that does all format generation in one pass, rather than running separate tools for HTML, EPUB, and PDF. The pattern: 1. **Load manuscript** → parse `## Chapter N — Title` headers into chapter list 2. **Build rich HTML** with cover (base64-embedded), copyright, TOC with chapter titles, all chapters, back cover 3. **Derive EPUB from the same HTML** — extract cover, copyright, TOC, chapter sections, and back matter from the HTML body using regex, then assemble EPUB3 structure (mimetype, container.xml, content.opf, nav.xhtml, per-chapter XHTML) 4. **Derive PDF from the same HTML** — pass directly to WeasyPrint: `HTML(string=html_content).write_pdf(output_path)` This approach ensures three formats are always in sync — no drift between HTML and EPUB/PDF content. ### Cover Embedding Technique Embed cover art as a base64 data URI so the HTML is fully self-contained (no external image files): ```python cover_file = os.path.join(cover_dir, f"{book_key}_Cover.png") if os.path.exists(cover_file): with open(cover_file, "rb") as f: cover_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode("utf-8") cover_img_html = f'' ``` For EPUB, include the cover image in the manifest with `properties="cover-image"` AND a separate cover XHTML in the spine. Both are required for KDP/Apple Books. ### CSS Pitfall: Blank Pages Before Every Chapter A common mistake: setting `page-break-before: always` on the general `h2` rule. Because chapter headings use `

    `, this inserts a blank page before every single chapter. **Fix:** Scope page breaks: ```css h2 { page-break-before: always; } /* structural h2 (copyright, TOC) */ .chapter-body h2 { page-break-before: avoid; margin-top: 1cm; } /* chapter titles */ ``` This keeps page breaks on structural elements (cover → copyright → TOC → chapters) while letting chapters flow naturally without leading blank pages. ### Text-Only Margins with Full-Bleed Art Breakout When a book contains chapter art that should extend to the page edges while body text sits at a defined margin, use `@page` margins for text and a CSS breakout class for images. #### Pattern ```css /* Text sits at 0.75in top/bottom, images can bleed past */ @page { size: 6in 9in; margin: 0.75in 0.8in; /* top/bottom, left/right — text margins */ @bottom-center { content: counter(page); } } /* Full-bleed art — negative margins extend past text margins to page edges */ .art, .full-bleed { margin: 0 -0.8in; /* cancel left/right margins horizontally */ width: calc(100% + 1.6in); /* extend past left+right margins combined */ max-width: none; display: block; } .art img, .full-bleed img { width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; } ``` #### How It Works - `@page margin: 0.75in 0.8in` sets the text content area 0.75" from top/bottom edges - The `.full-bleed` class uses negative left/right margins to break out of the content area - `calc(100% + 1.6in)` adds back the width consumed by the 0.8in left + 0.8in right margins, making the element span the full page width - Images set to `width: 100%; display: block` fill the breakout container edge-to-edge #### Usage in Manuscript HTML ```html

    Margaret stared at the holodisplay...

    The numbers didn't lie...

    ``` #### Pitfalls - **Margin values must match.** The `-0.8in` and `+1.6in` values in `.full-bleed` must exactly cancel the `@page` left/right margins. If you change page margins, recalculate both values. - **No `max-width: 100%`** — the breakout element is intentionally wider than its parent container. If a parent element has `max-width` or `overflow: hidden`, the breakout will be clipped. - **EPUB compatibility**: E-readers handle breakout differently. This technique works best in WeasyPrint PDFs. For EPUB, full-bleed art is less critical since e-readers typically scale images to screen width anyway. - **Page-edge art only left/right**: The `.full-bleed` class only breaks out horizontally (left/right). To have art break out of top/bottom margins too, add `margin-top: -0.75in` and `height: calc(...)` adjustments. Typically chapter art only needs horizontal bleed. - **Inline elements**: The `.full-bleed` class sets `display: block`. Do not apply it to inline elements or text spans. ### Duplicate Content Detection Across Series When restructuring a multi-series library, books from different series that share identical chapter titles are likely duplicates (same content, different character names). This happened with the No Blue Sky / Lunar Foundation series where Books 4/6 and 5/7 were identical. **Detection technique:** ```python # Compare chapter titles across books for book_a in series_a_books: for book_b in series_b_books: ch_titles_a = extract_chapter_titles(book_a) ch_titles_b = extract_chapter_titles(book_b) overlap = set(ch_titles_a) & set(ch_titles_b) if len(overlap) > len(ch_titles_a) * 0.8: print(f"DUPLICATE: {book_a} == {book_b}") ``` **Verification:** Even if chapter titles are identical, check body text for a shared unique string (e.g., a typo or Mission AI line) to confirm duplication. In one real case, a copy-paste error ("Chapter 36" instead of "Chapter 16") appeared in BOTH books across different series, conclusively proving they derived from the same source. **Remediation:** Rewrite one copy as a completely distinct story with different plot, characters, and genre (e.g., political thriller vs survival story vs mystery). The rewritten book must have a unique title, unique chapter sequence, and no shared narrative content. ### Page Count Compression (Content Trimming) After quality improvements add content, books may exceed the 180-200 page target. To compress without changing font size or margins: 1. **Extract full content** from the last clean PDF or HTML source 2. **Rebuild HTML from extracted text** using the original chapter structure 3. **Trim proportionally** — keep first ~85% of sentences per chapter, dropping redundant expansions 4. **Verify** by regenerating PDF and checking page count For aggressive compression, split scene-break sections and keep only the first 1-2 scenes per chapter. The opening + one development scene preserves the narrative arc while cutting filler. When splitting a single manuscript into multiple books at a chapter boundary (e.g., chapter 20/21, or splitting an already-split volume further): #### Finding the Split Point Analyze cumulative word counts per chapter to locate the target page boundary (250 words/page): ```python import re with open("manuscript.md") as f: content = f.read() chunks = re.split(r'^## Chapter (\d+)', content, flags=re.MULTILINE) chapters, current_num = {}, None for chunk in chunks: chunk = chunk.strip() if not chunk: continue if chunk.isdigit(): current_num = int(chunk) elif current_num is not None: chapters[current_num] = len(chunk.split()) cumulative, target_words = 0, 100 * 250 # target_pages * 250 for num in sorted(chapters): cumulative += chapters[num] if cumulative >= target_words: print(f"Split after Chapter {num}") break ``` #### The Split (with renumbering) Use `re.split()` on `## Chapter N — Title` headers, reconstruct the chapter list, then split at the boundary. For the **second book**, renumber chapters sequentially (Chapter 19 → Chapter 1, etc.) by targeting only header lines with `re.sub(r'Chapter \d+', f'Chapter {new_num}', ...)` — do NOT replace chapter numbers in body text or dialogue. #### Sequential/Recursive Splitting An already-split volume (e.g., "Part 2" that was itself the result of a previous split) can be split again into updated Part 2 + Part 3. Key considerations: - **Part 2 keeps its existing cover** (subtitle "PART 2" stays the same) — no need to regenerate unless the cover file naming changed - **Cover filename consistency check**: The cover generation script and publishing script must use the same filename prefix (e.g., both `Book_Part_2_Cover.png`, not `Book_Pt2_Cover.png` vs `Book_Part_2_Cover.png`) - **Part 3 needs a new cover** that visually advances the series aesthetic (different scene/subject, same typography style) #### Rewriting Boundary Chapters The split point needs two targeted rewrites: **Book 1's last chapter** — rewrite as a series-ending chapter: - A closing arc that resolves the book's central tension - Characters reflecting on how far they've come (viewport/observation scene optional but effective) - A thematic callback to the series title - A bridge paragraph (italic, marked as "Bridge" or "End of Book N") that sets up what's coming in the next book - The closing should feel like a chapter end AND a book end **Book 2's first chapter** — rewrite the opening to include: - A **book-level Mission AI ping** using the convention: `Mission AI: "Book N — Chapter 1: [thematic summary]"` — this distinguishes it from regular chapter-level Mission AI lines - A **summary transition paragraph** (the "bridge" from Book 1's cliffhanger or resolution) that re-establishes setting and stakes - The original chapter's content — keep it intact, only replace the opening lines - A character quote that reflects the new book's theme **Common pitfall — duplicate Mission AI lines:** When inserting new book-opening content before the original Chapter 1's `*Mission AI: ...*` line, the old opening lines survive and create duplicates. After inserting the new opening, **always check for and remove** the old duplicate Mission AI + character quote pair that immediately follows. #### Chapter Header Parser Pitfall Some manuscripts have two `##` lines per chapter (bare `## Chapter N` followed by `## Chapter N — Title`). Match only `## Chapter N — Title` (with dash/title after the number) to avoid double-splitting. #### Regenerate After splitting and rewriting, regenerate all three formats (HTML, EPUB, PDF) for both books from their respective manuscripts using the Integrated Single-Script Pipeline above. ## Troubleshooting **Issue**: Images not generating properly **Solution**: Refine prompts with more specific details, try different AI models **Issue**: PDF formatting breaks or looks wrong **Solution**: Check CSS for print-specific rules, ensure proper page breaks, validate HTML structure. Most common fix: scope `page-break-before` to structural elements only, not generic h2. **Issue**: WeasyPrint not available or not working **Solution**: Use browser print method or install wkhtmltopdf as alternative **Issue**: Images not displaying in PDF **Solution**: Check file paths, ensure images are accessible, use absolute paths if needed. For self-contained HTML, use base64 data URIs — they always resolve regardless of filesystem context. **Issue**: EPUB shows duplicate chapters or wrong number of chapters **Solution**: The EPUB generator extracts chapters from the final HTML using regex. If the manuscript has two `##` lines per chapter (e.g., `## Chapter N` plus `## Chapter N — Title`), the regex may split on both. The HTML and EPUB will send fine together; send the PDF in its own follow-up message. ## Notes This workflow combines traditional publishing approaches with modern AI tools. The key is maintaining the author's voice while leveraging technology to enhance quality and efficiency. ## Appending External Content as an Appendix When a user provides an external PDF (case study, research paper, article) to include as an appendix in an existing book, use this workflow: ### When to Use - A PDF document (case study, whitepaper, interview transcript) needs to be appended to the end of a completed manuscript - The user wants to expand a book with new material without modifying the original chapters - Back cover needs updating with review blurbs from partner companies or endorsers ### Step 1: Extract PDF to Markdown Use `pdftotext` (from poppler-utils) to extract the text, then clean up PDF artifacts: ```bash pdftotext "/path/to/document.pdf" - > /tmp/extracted.txt ``` **Common PDF artifacts to clean:** - Spaced-out capital letters: `A C A S E S T U D Y` → replace with the properly spaced form - Page numbers on their own lines: skip lines that are just a number < 5 digits - Table of Contents sections: skip entries that list chapters with page numbers - Part/chapter header formatting: normalize to markdown heading levels (`##`, `###`) - Repeated title/author blocks at chapter starts ### Step 2: Build the Combined HTML Write (or extend an existing) build script that: 1. **Reads the original manuscript** (markdown with `## Chapter N` headers) 2. **Extracts the appendix content** from the cleaned markdown 3. **Builds HTML structured as:** Cover → Title → Copyright → TOC → Chapters → Appendix → Back Cover **CSS sections to add:** ```css .appendix { page-break-before: always; } .appendix h2 { font-size: 20pt; text-align: center; } .appendix h3 { font-size: 16pt; margin-top: 25px; } .back-cover { page-break-before: always; background-color: #000000; color: #ffffff; text-align: center; padding: 60px 40px; min-height: 600px; } .back-cover .review { font-style: italic; font-size: 13pt; margin: 30px 0; color: #e0e0e0; } .back-cover .review-author { font-style: normal; font-size: 11pt; color: #aaaaaa; } .back-cover hr { border: none; border-top: 1px solid #444; margin: 30px 60px; } ``` ### Step 3: Build the Back Cover The back cover typically includes: - Book title (white, large) - Subtitle (white, smaller, italic) - 2-3 review blurbs from endorsers (italic white on black, 13pt) - Reviewer attribution (smaller, gray) - Publisher/imprint branding at bottom ### Step 4: Avoid Duplicate TOCs If the original markdown has a TOC section AND the build script generates one programmatically, you'll get two TOCs in the output. **Remove the programmatic TOC generation** in the build script and rely on the markdown's own TOC. Update the markdown TOC to include the appendix entry. ### Step 5: Generate the Combined Package ```python # Key structure for the build script: html_parts = [ # Front matter (cover, title, copyright) — hardcoded # TOC — from markdown or single programmatic version # Chapters — from original manuscript, unchanged # Appendix — from extracted PDF markdown, with .appendix CSS class # Back cover — hardcoded black background with reviews ] ``` Save to the manuscript's final print HTML path. Also save a combined markdown version with `## Appendix:` header added at the end. ### Pitfalls - **PDF extraction quality**: `pdftotext` may mangle columns, tables, or complex layouts. Always review the extracted text for artifact lines (page numbers, TOC lists, header/footer repeats). - **Second TOC**: When adding an appendix, update the TOC to include it. If there are TWO TOCs (one in markdown, one programmatic), remove the programmatic one to avoid duplicates. - **Back cover CSS isolation**: The `.back-cover` styles must NOT inherit from the body styles. Mission AI had sequenced the startup perfectly, as it always did. The generator hummed at 98.7 percent efficiency, producing 34 kilowatts of continuous power that would keep the batteries charged and the life‑support systems running when the dust came.

The mission timeline was stored in Mission AI's memory banks as a sequence of numbered sol events — Sol 0 for landing, Sol 720 for the scheduled departure window, Sol 730 for Earth return. The logic was simple and brutal: two years on Mars, then home. Everything from food packaging to suit rotation schedules had been built around that assumption. The return ship — the vessel that would carry thirty people back to orbit, where the homeward fleet would be waiting — was a separate spacecraft that would arrive at Mars orbit six months before the crew was scheduled to leave the surface.

Review the conversation above and update two things:

**Memory**: who the user is. Did the user reveal persona, desires, preferences, personal details, or expectations about how you should behave? Save facts about the user and durable preferences with the memory tool.

**Skills**: how to do this class of task. Be ACTIVE — most sessions produce at least one skill update. A pass that does nothing is a missed learning opportunity, not a neutral outcome.

Target shape of the skill library: CLASS-LEVEL skills with a rich SKILL.md and a `references/` directory for session-specific detail. Not a long flat list of narrow one-session-one-skill entries.

Signals that warrant a skill update (any one is enough):
  • User corrected your style, tone, format, legibility, verbosity, or approach. Frustration is a FIRST-CLASS skill signal, not just a memory signal. 'stop doing X', 'don't format like this', 'I hate when you Y' — embed the lesson in the skill that governs that task so the next session starts fixed.
  • Non-trivial technique, fix, workaround, or debugging path emerged.
  • A skill that was loaded or consulted turned out wrong, missing, or outdated — patch it now.

Preference order for skills — pick the earliest that fits:
  1. UPDATE A CURRENTLY-LOADED SKILL. Check what skills were loaded via /skill-name or skill_view in the conversation. If one of them covers the learning, PATCH it first. It was in play; it's the right place.
  2. UPDATE AN EXISTING UMBRELLA (skills_list + skill_view to find the right one). Patch it.
  3. ADD A SUPPORT FILE under an existing umbrella via skill_manage action=write_file. Three kinds: `references/<topic>.md` for session-specific detail OR condensed knowledge banks (quoted research, API docs excerpts, domain notes) written concise and task-focused; `templates/<name>.<ext>` for starter files meant to be copied and modified; `scripts/<name>.<ext>` for statically re-runnable actions (verification, fixture generators, probes). Add a one-line pointer in SKILL.md so future agents find them.
  4. CREATE A NEW CLASS-LEVEL UMBRELLA when nothing exists. Name at the class level — NOT a PR number, error string, codename, library-alone name, or 'fix-X / debug-Y' session artifact. If the name only fits today's task, fall back to (1), (2), or (3).

User-preference embedding: when the user complains about how you handled a task, update the skill that governs that task — memory alone isn't enough. Memory says 'who the user is and what the current situation and state of your operations are'; skills say 'how to do this class of task for this user'. Both should carry user-preference lessons when relevant.

If you notice overlapping existing skills, mention it — the background curator handles consolidation.

Do NOT capture as skills (these become persistent self-imposed constraints that bite you later when the environment changes):
  • Environment-dependent failures: missing binaries, fresh-install errors, post-migration path mismatches, 'command not found', unconfigured credentials, uninstalled packages. The user can fix these — they are not durable rules.
  • Negative claims about tools or features ('browser tools do not work', 'X tool is broken', 'cannot use Y from execute_code'). These harden into refusals the agent cites against itself for months after the actual problem was fixed.
  • Session-specific transient errors that resolved before the conversation ended. If retrying worked, the lesson is the retry pattern, not the original failure.
  • One-off task narratives. A user asking 'summarize today's market' or 'analyze this PR' is not a class of work that warrants a skill.

If a tool failed because of setup state, capture the FIX (install command, config step, env var to set) under an existing setup or troubleshooting skill — never 'this tool does not work' as a standalone constraint.

Act on whichever of the two dimensions has real signal. If genuinely nothing stands out on either, say 'Nothing to save.' and stop — but don't reach for that conclusion as a default.

The EPUB builder must detect all of them. ## Four Formats Found in Production ### Format 1: `

Chapter ...

` wrapper (Books 6–8) ```html

Chapter 1 — The Observatory Rising

Chapter 2

``` Some editions show CHAPTER NUMBER ONLY on one div (no title text), followed by a second div with the full chapter title. Both are chapters. Detected by: `

Chapter ...

Contents
